title: Reading a temporal bone CT
summary: The axial ladder from the superior canal down to the jugular bulb, then the coronal ladder from the carotid back to the mastoid. Learn the level each structure appears at, so a single slice tells you where you are.

steps.title: Start at the top: the superior canal
steps.text: Scrolling down from the middle fossa, the first labyrinthine structure is the superior semicircular canal: two dots, then a ring, under the arcuate eminence. The tegmen and attic are lateral to it.

steps.title: The attic and the ice-cream cone
steps.text: A few slices down, the epitympanum contains the malleus head (the scoop, anterior) and the incus body with its short process (the cone, posterior). The aditus leads back to the antrum, and the lateral canal is about to appear on the medial wall.

steps.title: IAC, vestibule, lateral canal
steps.text: The key slice. The IAC runs in from the posterior petrous surface to the fundus; the vestibule sits lateral to the fundus; the lateral canal arcs posterolaterally from it. The facial nerve's labyrinthine segment leaves the fundus anterolaterally toward the geniculate.

steps.title: Cochlea and oval window
steps.text: One or two slices lower, the cochlea's turns appear anterior to the vestibule with the carotid genu anterior to them. The oval window and stapes bridge the vestibule and the middle ear, with the facial nerve's tympanic segment running just above on the slice before this one.

steps.title: Round window and the hypotympanum
steps.text: The basal turn's posterior end opens into the round window niche, facing the hypotympanum. The facial nerve's mastoid segment is now a round canal posterior to the facial recess, and the sinus tympani is the pocket medial to it.

steps.title: Jugular bulb and carotid
steps.text: At the bottom of the ladder: the jugular bulb posterolateral, the carotid canal anteromedial, with the caroticojugular spine between. Note the bony floor of the hypotympanum over the bulb; absence means dehiscence.

steps.title: Coronal ladder, front to back: carotid and Eustachian tube
steps.text: Switch to coronal and start anteriorly. The vertical carotid canal sits anteromedial to the middle ear; the Eustachian tube and tensor tympani leave the protympanum above it.

steps.title: The oval window stack
steps.text: The most important coronal slice: from top to bottom, the scutum and attic laterally, the lateral canal, the facial nerve tympanic segment, the oval window with the stapes, and the promontory. Memorise this vertical order; it is how you read facial nerve dehiscence and fenestral otosclerosis.

steps.title: Vestibule and the posterior canal
steps.text: Further back, the vestibule is a smooth oval with the posterior canal and common crus behind it and the IAC medial. The incus long process descends toward the stapes lateral to the window.

steps.title: Mastoid segment and jugular bulb
steps.text: The posterior slices show the facial nerve's whole descent from the second genu to the stylomastoid foramen, with the jugular bulb medial and inferior and the sigmoid behind the mastoid cells.

title: Facial nerve from the porus to the stylomastoid foramen
summary: Follow the nerve through its four intratemporal segments and the landmarks that locate each one. Every segment has a surgical approach that finds it and a classic injury that threatens it.

steps.title: Porus and the meatal segment
steps.text: The nerve enters the IAC at the porus and runs laterally along its anterosuperior wall, 8-10 mm, accompanied by the nervus intermedius, cochlear and vestibular nerves and the labyrinthine artery.

steps.title: The fundus: Bill's bar and the transverse crest
steps.text: At the lateral end the transverse crest splits the fundus into upper and lower halves and Bill's bar separates the facial nerve (anterior) from the superior vestibular nerve (posterior). The meatal foramen here is the narrowest point of the whole nerve.

steps.title: Labyrinthine segment
steps.text: The shortest and narrowest segment runs anterolaterally between the cochlea below and the superior canal ampulla behind, to the geniculate ganglion. No anastomotic blood supply, a tight canal, and the site of Bell's palsy compression.

steps.title: Geniculate ganglion and the GSPN
steps.text: At the first genu the nerve turns sharply posteriorly. The greater superficial petrosal nerve leaves anteromedially under the middle fossa dura; the ganglion is dehiscent into the middle fossa in a notable minority, which is why dura is elevated from posterior to anterior.

steps.title: Tympanic segment: cochleariform process
steps.text: The nerve emerges just above and behind the cochleariform process, the most reliable landmark when the oval window is obscured. It runs posteriorly along the medial wall of the attic and mesotympanum.

steps.title: Tympanic segment: over the oval window
steps.text: Here the nerve lies directly above the stapes footplate and below the lateral canal. This is where it is dehiscent in roughly half of temporal bones histologically, and where stapes surgery and cholesteatoma dissection endanger it.

steps.title: Second genu
steps.text: Below the posterior limb of the lateral canal and lateral to the posterior canal, the nerve turns inferiorly. The short process of the incus in the fossa incudis points at it from 2-3 mm lateral and superior; the pyramidal eminence is just anterior.

steps.title: Mastoid segment and the chorda
steps.text: The vertical segment descends 10-14 mm lateral to the posterior canal and medial to the posterior canal wall. The chorda tympani leaves it a few millimetres above the foramen and runs forward to enter the middle ear; the facial recess lies between the two.

steps.title: Stylomastoid foramen
steps.text: The nerve exits anterior to the anterior end of the digastric ridge and posterolateral to the styloid base. In infants without a mastoid tip it is superficial here; in adults the tragal pointer and tympanomastoid suture locate it for parotid surgery.

title: Mastoidectomy landmarks in order
summary: The landmarks of a cortical mastoidectomy in the order a surgeon meets them, with the three preoperative CT checks that prevent surprises: sigmoid position, tegmen height and Korner's septum.

steps.title: MacEwen's triangle
steps.text: The first burr cut centres on the suprameatal triangle: below the temporal line, behind the posterosuperior canal margin. The antrum lies 12-15 mm deep in an adult and only 2-4 mm in a newborn.

steps.title: Tegmen
steps.text: Identify the middle fossa plate early as the superior limit and keep the burr parallel to it. A low tegmen narrows the attic entrance; small dehiscences are common and harmless if the dura is not violated.

steps.title: Sigmoid sinus and the sinodural angle
steps.text: The posterior limit. Thin the sinus plate to a blue line and open the sinodural angle fully; retained cells here are the classic incomplete mastoidectomy. An anteriorly placed sinus (under 10 mm from the canal wall) crowds everything.

steps.title: The antrum and Korner's septum
steps.text: Deepen the dissection to the antrum. If a vertical bony plate is met before a large cell with a bulge in its medial wall, it is Korner's septum and the true antrum lies medial to it. The lateral canal prominence is the proof.

steps.title: Lateral semicircular canal
steps.text: The first labyrinthine landmark: a smooth, dense bulge in the medial wall of the antrum. Once seen, the facial nerve is known to lie below and anterior, and Donaldson's line can be projected posteriorly to the sigmoid.

steps.title: Fossa incudis and the short process
steps.text: Open the aditus forward to find the short process of the incus. The facial nerve's second genu is 2-3 mm inferomedial to its tip; the burr stays lateral and below it.

steps.title: Facial nerve: second genu and mastoid segment
steps.text: With the lateral canal above and the fossa incudis lateral, thin the bone over the nerve with a diamond burr, drilling parallel to its course. The nerve becomes visible as a pink-grey line through thin bone.

steps.title: Digastric ridge and the mastoid tip
steps.text: Exenterate the tip cells down to the digastric ridge. Follow the ridge anteriorly: the stylomastoid foramen and the nerve are at its anterior end, 1-2 mm anterior to it.

steps.title: Trautmann's triangle and the endolymphatic sac
steps.text: Between the sigmoid, the labyrinth and the superior petrosal sinus is the posterior fossa dura. Below Donaldson's line, the thickened dura is the endolymphatic sac; retrofacial cells between the nerve and the posterior canal lead to it.

title: Posterior tympanotomy, the windows and the sinus tympani
curriculum: Otology: cochlear implantation and chronic ear surgery
summary: The facial recess corridor from the mastoid to the middle ear: its three boundaries, what you see through it, what you cannot see (the sinus tympani), and the trajectory to the round window for a cochlear implant.

steps.title: The three boundaries
steps.text: The facial recess is bounded by the facial nerve's mastoid segment medially, the chorda tympani laterally and the fossa incudis above. Its usual width is 2-3 mm; the chorda can be sacrificed for another millimetre or two.

steps.title: Opening the recess
steps.text: Thin the bone between the nerve and the chorda from the fossa incudis downward with a small diamond burr, staying lateral to the nerve. Widen inferiorly: the round window niche is lower than most residents expect.

steps.title: Stapes and the oval window
steps.text: Through the upper recess the stapes, pyramidal eminence and stapedius tendon come into view, with the facial nerve's tympanic segment running above the window.

steps.title: Round window niche
steps.text: Inferiorly and anteriorly the niche appears as a dark recess under its bony overhang. Drill the overhang to see the membrane's full circumference; a mucosal fold can masquerade as the membrane.

steps.title: Trajectory into the cochlea
steps.text: The electrode goes through the membrane along the basal turn, anteroinferiorly toward the carotid, not straight medially. Record the A value and cochlear patency on the preoperative CT.

steps.title: Sinus tympani: what the recess cannot show
steps.text: Medial to the pyramidal eminence and the nerve lies the sinus tympani, invisible through the facial recess. Classify its depth on CT (Marchioni A, B or C); a type C sinus posterior to the nerve needs an endoscope or a retrofacial approach.

steps.title: Check the jugular bulb
steps.text: A high bulb can sit under the round window niche or fill the retrofacial space. It is the structure that most often changes the plan: check its dome on coronal images before the operation.

title: Inner ear and the internal auditory canal
curriculum: Otology and neurotology: labyrinth and IAC
summary: The bony labyrinth piece by piece, then the IAC and its two aqueducts. This tour pairs with the pre-implant and pre-skull-base CT checklist.

steps.title: Cochlear turns
steps.text: Two and a half turns around the modiolus, the apex pointing anterolaterally. The basal turn is largest, forms the promontory laterally, and ends posteriorly at the round window.

steps.title: Modiolus and the cochlear aperture
steps.text: The cochlear nerve enters the modiolus from the anteroinferior fundus through the cochlear aperture; its width (about 2 mm normally, stenotic under about 1.4 mm) is a marker of cochlear nerve deficiency.

steps.title: Vestibule
steps.text: The central chamber, oval on every plane, with the oval window on its lateral wall. Utricle posterosuperiorly, saccule anteroinferiorly under the footplate's posterior half.

steps.title: Three canals and the common crus
steps.text: Lateral canal roughly horizontal, superior canal perpendicular to the petrous axis, posterior canal parallel to the posterior petrous surface. The superior and posterior canals share the common crus, so five openings reach the vestibule.

steps.title: Vestibular aqueduct and the sac
steps.text: Leaving the posteromedial vestibule parallel to the posterior canal, the aqueduct reaches the operculum on the posterior petrous surface and the endolymphatic sac. Measure its midpoint on axial images: 1 mm or more is enlarged by the Cincinnati criteria.

steps.title: Cochlear aqueduct
steps.text: From the basal turn near the round window, the perilymphatic channel runs medially below the IAC to the posterior fossa near the jugular foramen. Corticated, predictable, not a fracture.

steps.title: IAC and its contents
steps.text: Eight to ten millimetres from the porus to the fundus; symmetric width within a millimetre or two of the other side. Facial nerve anterosuperior, cochlear anteroinferior, vestibular nerves posterior; the transverse crest and Bill's bar divide them at the fundus.

title: Vascular hazards: carotid, jugular bulb, sigmoid
curriculum: Otology and neurotology: vascular anatomy of the temporal bone
summary: Where the three great vessels run, how thin the bone over each is, and the variants that turn a routine middle ear or mastoid case into a vascular emergency.

steps.title: Vertical carotid
steps.text: The carotid enters anteromedial to the jugular bulb and rises anterior to the hypotympanum and protympanum, separated from the middle ear by thin bone. The caroticojugular spine separates it from the bulb.

steps.title: Carotid genu and the cochlea
steps.text: At the genu the artery turns anteromedially beneath the cochlea; often under a millimetre of bone separates the two. The Eustachian tube and tensor tympani lie lateral to the horizontal segment.

steps.title: Jugular bulb and the hypotympanum
steps.text: The bulb's dome is normally below the hypotympanic floor and the basal turn. Judge its height on coronal images relative to the round window; a dehiscent bulb is a blue mass behind the inferior drum.

steps.title: Sigmoid sinus
steps.text: The posterior boundary of the mastoid, bisected by Donaldson's line, joined by the superior petrosal sinus at the sinodural angle. Its distance from the posterior canal wall is the first number on a pre-mastoidectomy CT.

steps.title: Emissary vein
steps.text: The mastoid emissary vein leaves the sigmoid through the posterior cortex. It bleeds in the postauricular approach and tells you where the sinus is before the first cut.

steps.title: Variants that bite
steps.text: Aberrant carotid (absent vertical canal, vessel on the promontory), persistent stapedial artery (absent foramen spinosum, widened facial canal), high or dehiscent jugular bulb, sigmoid diverticulum. Any red or blue retrotympanic mass gets a CT before an instrument touches it.

title: Dangerous variants: the preoperative checklist
summary: A structured pass through the variants that change an operation. Each step shows where to look on the CT and states the finding to report.

steps.title: Facial nerve dehiscence at the oval window
steps.text: Look on coronal images above the footplate. Dehiscence is present in about half of bones histologically and CT underestimates it; an exposed or overhanging nerve changes stapes surgery and cholesteatoma dissection.

steps.title: Anterior facial nerve in atresia
steps.text: In congenital aural atresia the mastoid segment runs anteriorly and laterally and may cross the round window or the planned canal. The Jahrsdoerfer score counts it.

steps.title: High or dehiscent jugular bulb
steps.text: Coronal: dome above the inferior annulus, the basal turn or the round window niche by the various definitions. Blocks the round window approach, the retrofacial approach and the retrosigmoid IAC exposure.

steps.title: Aberrant carotid and persistent stapedial artery
steps.text: Absent vertical carotid canal with a vessel crossing the promontory; absent foramen spinosum with an enlarged tympanic facial canal. Both present as a red retrotympanic mass and both can be catastrophic if biopsied.

steps.title: Anterior sigmoid and low tegmen
steps.text: Sagittal and axial: sigmoid under 10 mm from the posterior canal wall and a middle fossa floor at or below the lateral canal level. Together they can make a canal-wall-up mastoidectomy impractical.

steps.title: Superior canal dehiscence
steps.text: Never call it on axial or coronal alone. Reformat in the Poschl and Stenvers planes at 0.5 mm or thinner; about 0.5% of bones are dehiscent and more are thin. Correlate with VEMPs and symptoms.

steps.title: Enlarged vestibular aqueduct
steps.text: Midpoint 1 mm or more, or operculum 2 mm or more. Associated with Pendred, incomplete partition II and stepwise hearing loss after minor trauma. Add MRI to see the sac.

steps.title: Korner's septum
steps.text: A vertical petrosquamous plate lateral to the antrum in roughly a fifth of bones. The lateral compartment is a false antrum; the lateral canal proves the real one.

steps.title: Hyrtl's fissure
steps.text: A persistent tympanomeningeal cleft from the round window niche to the posterior fossa: a rare cause of CSF otorrhoea and recurrent meningitis with a normal labyrinth.

steps.title: Cochlear malformations, IAC and cochlear aperture
steps.text: Count the turns and check the modiolus (incomplete partition I-III), measure the IAC (stenotic under 2 mm) and the cochlear aperture (under 1.4 mm). These decide implant feasibility and gusher risk.

title: Middle fossa and translabyrinthine landmarks
summary: The two classic routes to the IAC: from above through the middle fossa with hearing preserved, and from behind through the labyrinth with hearing sacrificed. Each has a sequence of landmarks that must be found in order.

steps.title: Middle fossa: arcuate eminence
steps.text: After the temporal craniotomy and dural elevation from posterior to anterior, the arcuate eminence marks the approximate position of the superior canal. It is unreliable: blue-line the canal.

steps.title: Middle fossa: GSPN
steps.text: Anteromedial to the eminence the greater superficial petrosal nerve runs under the dura in the facial hiatus. Traction on it means traction on the geniculate; follow it posteriorly to the ganglion.

steps.title: Middle fossa: finding the IAC
steps.text: Fisch's meatal plane lies 60 degrees from the superior canal; Garcia-Ibanez bisects the GSPN-superior canal angle; House follows the GSPN to the geniculate and the labyrinthine segment medially. The canal is unroofed from medial to lateral, where Bill's bar separates facial from superior vestibular nerve.

steps.title: Translabyrinthine: sigmoid decompression
steps.text: A complete mastoidectomy, then the sigmoid is skeletonised and the sinodural angle opened so the sinus can be retracted; the posterior fossa dura is exposed to the porus.

steps.title: Translabyrinthine: labyrinthectomy in order
steps.text: Lateral canal first, then superior and posterior canals to the common crus, then the vestibule. The facial nerve is skeletonised at the second genu before the canals are opened, and the subarcuate artery is expected inside the superior canal's arc.

steps.title: Translabyrinthine: the IAC
steps.text: From the vestibule the fundus is reached medially; the canal is skeletonised over 180-270 degrees between the jugular bulb below and the middle fossa dura above. The superior vestibular nerve, then Bill's bar, then the facial nerve.

steps.title: Translabyrinthine: the inferior limit
steps.text: The cochlear aqueduct marks the lower edge of the IAC dissection and the position of the glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen; opening it releases CSF and lowers the brain.
